query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A thin, fluorine‐based surface treatment will induce the formation of a continuous and adherent Al2O3 protective layer on cast HfNbTaTiZr, thereby reducing its oxygen uptake at high temperature without compromising its mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but exhibiting poor oxygen resistance during high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Apply a fluorine-based surface treatment (for example, spraying or dipping the alloy in a dilute NH4F aqueous solution) to modify the surface chemistry, followed by controlled isothermal oxidation treatment.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C in ambient air for approximately 100 hours; mechanical performance to be evaluated at room temperature and under high-temperature tensile conditions (strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1)).
generation.structural_mediator: The fluorine treatment promotes the formation of a dense, continuous Al2O3 layer that adheres strongly to the substrate, effectively inhibiting further oxygen diffusion.
generation.mechanism: The surface fluorine reacts (or modifies the local oxidation kinetics) to favor the selective formation of Al2O3 over less-protective oxides. This protective oxide scale reduces oxygen ingress and subsequent degradation, while leaving the bulk microstructure and its beneficial mechanical properties intact.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the treated specimens should exhibit a significantly reduced oxidation weight gain and enhanced oxidation resistance at 1000 °C, while retaining similar tensile ductility and yield strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: Untreated, cast HfNbTaTiZr demonstrates poor oxygen resistance, limiting its high‐temperature applications despite its acceptable mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: If the fluorine treatment is too aggressive (i.e., if concentration or exposure time is not optimized), it may lead to detrimental surface modifications or embrittlement, potentially affecting ductility or strength.
generation.uncertainty: Although similar fluorine treatments have improved oxidation resistance in Ti–Al–Nb alloys, the optimal treatment parameters and the resulting oxide layer characteristics for HfNbTaTiZr are not yet established and may differ due to its unique composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr cast specimens: one set receives the optimized fluorine-based surface treatment and the other remains untreated. Subject both sets to an isothermal oxidation test at 1000 °C in ambient air for 100 hours. After exposure, conduct mass-gain measurements and detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM, XRD) to assess the oxide scale formation. In parallel, perform tensile mechanical tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C (using strain rates between 10^(-4) and 10^(-2) s^(-1)).
measurements: Phase and microstructure analysis of the oxide layer (SEM, XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fluorine-treated specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar mass gain and oxide morphology as the untreated samples) or if their tensile properties (ductility and yield strength) are adversely altered compared to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In-depth analyses of the anti-oxidation behavior and structure of γ-TiAl alloys are of great significant for their maintenance and repair in engineering applications. In this work, fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects were prepared by isothermal oxidation treatment at 1000 °C. Several characterization methods, including SEM, EDS, XRD and TEM, were used to evaluate the surface microstructure of the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects. The results indicate that the fluorine promoted the formation of an outer protective film of Al2O3, which significantly improved the oxidation resistance. The microcracks of oxidized specimens with the artificial defects provided a rapid diffusion passage for Ti and O elements during the 1000 °C/2 h isothermal oxidation treatment process, resulting in the quick growth of TiO2 toward the outside. The fine Al2O3 constituted a continuous film after the 1000 °C/100 h isothermal oxidation treatment. In this study, we executed a simple and effective strategy involving a two-step spraying and oxidation process to produce Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys with a dense Al2O3 film for application at high temperatures. The main results are as follows: (1)The oxidation resistance was significantly improved due to the formation of a protective Al2O3 film induced by the fluorine effect during isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C (6.03 mg/cm2 weight gain for the bare Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys, but 0.81 mg/cm2 for the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys).(2)The Ti diffused along the artificial microcracks, resulting in a quick growth of TiO2 in a short time (2 h), while a continuous Al2O3 film was generated underneath the oxide scale during further isothermal oxidation (100 h).(3)The Al2O3 particles between the alloy and continuous Al2O3 film were reflected in the γ-TiAl and α2-Ti3Al phases, which improved the adhesion of the oxide scale (fluorine-treated specimen had a deep yellow oxide scale on the surface without any exfoliation). These findings represent significant progress towards reducing the high temperature oxidation resistance of TiAl intermetallics by surface fluorine modification.
